# Vectors

## A vector stores many values of one type

```{r}
scores <- c(45, 62, 78)
scores
```

- One name for many values
- Values stay in order
- One object in memory

::: notes
A vector is the basic way R stores values. In fact, also singletons are really vectors of length one.
:::

## Mixed values are coerced

If you try to mix values, R will force them to a common type:

```{r}
survey_answers <- c(1, 2, "3")
survey_answers
```

```{r}
typeof(survey_answers)
```

- One vector, one type
- Coercion can be silent and cause bugs

::: notes
When mixed values are combined, they are coerced to a common type according to a hierarchy. R tries to preserve information, but sometimes the coercion can hide a mistake.
:::

## Logical operators evaluate each pair of elements

```{r}
scores >= 60
```

```{r}
scores >= 60 & scores < 75
```

- Same operators as before
- One result per element: a logical vector

```{r}
typeof(scores >= 60)
```

::: notes
The operators are familiar from lecture 3, but the result is now a logical vector rather than one single logical value.
:::

## Be wary of recycling

```{r}
#| warning: true
c(1, 2, 3) > c(1, 3)
```

- Shorter vector may repeat
- Sometimes warning
- Sometimes silent

::: notes
Recycling can be convenient, but it can also hide a mistake. Length mismatches deserve suspicion.
:::

## Boolean operators also recycle

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
#| warning: true
c(TRUE, FALSE) | c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```
::: fragment
`&&` and `||` are different: they only look at the first element and are meant for scalar conditions.

```{r}
TRUE || FALSE
```

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
#| error: true
c(TRUE, FALSE) || c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```
:::

::: notes
`&` and `|` work element by element and follow the same recycling rules as other vectorized operators. `&&` and `||` only inspect the first element, which is why they are the right operators inside `if / else` conditions. If vectors are supplied to `&&` or `||`, R uses the first element and warns.
:::

## "Vectorized" functions operate element by element

```{r}
#| output-location: default
trial <- c(1, NA, 3)
is.na(trial)
!is.na(trial)
```

- Same `is.na()`
- One result per element
- Useful before filtering

::: notes
Not all functions take vector inputs. The missingness tools from lecture 3 become more useful once many values are handled at once. This pattern shows up constantly in data cleaning.
:::

## Use `%in%` to check membership

```{r}
#| output-location: default
cities <- c("stockholm", "uppsala", "umea")
cities %in% c("stockholm", "malmo", "uppsala")
```

- Membership in a reference set
- One result per element


Often clearer than many `|`:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
cities == "stockholm" | cities == "malmo" | cities == "uppsala"
```

::: notes
`%in%` is especially useful when checking whether values belong to an allowed set of categories, identifiers, or years.
:::

## `ifelse()` builds a new vector

The `if / else` pattern requires `condition` to be a single logical value. If you want to apply the same logic to many values, `ifelse()` is the vectorized alternative:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
ifelse(scores >= 60, "pass", "retry")
```

- Condition checked element by element
- Output has matching length
- Useful for quick categories

## Subset vectors *by position* with `[]`

```{r}
years <- c(2021, 2022, 2023, 2024)
```

Integer vector inside `[]` subsets by position.

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
years[1]
```

Negative indices drop positions:

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
years[c(-3, -4)]
```

::: aside
We can use `:` to create a sequence of integers, which is often useful for subsetting by position; for example `years[2:4]` gives us the second through fourth elements of the `years` vector. Try it!
:::

## Subset vectors *by logical vector* with `[]`

Use a same-length logical vector to keep matching elements:
```{r}
#| output-location: default
years[c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)]
```

## Subset vectors *by condition* with `[]`

Or let a condition evaluate to a logical vector on the fly:

```{r}
scores[scores >= 60]
```

```{r}
years[years >= 2023]
```

This is what we use to filter table rows!

## Vectors can replace loops

```{r}
out <- numeric(length(scores))
for (i in seq_along(scores)) {
  out[i] <- scores[i]^2
}
out
```

```{r}
scores^2
```

- Same result
- Loop is explicit
- Vector form is shorter and often faster

::: notes
The point is not that loops are wrong. The point is that many operations in R already know how to work element by element on a whole vector, so the shorter vector form is often easier to read and write.
:::

## A list can hold different kinds of objects

```{r}
#| output-location: default
student_record <- list(name = "Alice", age = 24, passed = TRUE)
student_record
typeof(student_record)
```

- Flexible container
- Mixed object types allowed

::: notes
Lists are more flexible than atomic vectors because their elements do not all need the same type.
:::

# From Vectors To Tables

## Start with three column vectors

A table is really just a collection of equal-length vectors. Let's build one:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
municipality_code <- c("0180", "1280")
year <- c(2023, 2023)
unemployment_rate <- c(6.2, 7.1)
```

## Collect them in a list

```{r}
table_list <- list(
  municipality_code,
  year,
  unemployment_rate
)
table_list
```

## Give the columns names

```{r}
table_list <- list(
  municipality_code = municipality_code,
  year = year,
  unemployment_rate = unemployment_rate
)
table_list
```

::: notes
The ingredients of a simple table are just equal-length vectors. Before there is any table syntax, there are already ordinary vectors in memory.
:::

## Data frames

`data.frame()` is the built-in way of doing this

```{r}
table_df <- data.frame(
  municipality_code,
  year,
  unemployment_rate
)
table_df
```

Note how the naming is implicit.

::: notes
A `data.frame` is built by combining equal-length vectors into one tabular object. Unlike `list()`, `data.frame()` requires compatible lengths — it will recycle shorter vectors only if their length evenly divides the longest, and error otherwise.
:::

## Under the hood

`data.frame` is just a named equal-length list:

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
typeof(table_df)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
str(table_df)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
str(table_list)
```


::: notes
The difference is that `data.frame` has a different `class`. The special class `data.frame` adds table behavior to an underlying list. For example, the class comes with its own print method (`print.data.frame`) that shows the list in a tabular format.
:::

## A matrix is something else

Matrices are also rectangular, but they hold one common type:

```{r}
as.matrix(table_df)
```

```{r}
typeof(as.matrix(table_df))
```

- Still rows and columns, but stored as a single vector
- One common type for all cells

::: notes
A matrix is closer to one atomic vector with dimensions than to a list of column vectors. That is why matrices are useful for numeric linear algebra.
:::

## A first data set example

Let's work with the municipal panel data from lecture 1:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df <- read.csv("../lecture_1/lecture_1_demo_panel.csv")
head(panel_df)
```

## Inspect first

```{r}
#| output-location: default
str(panel_df)
```

Try `View(panel_df)` in VS Code / Positron for an interactive viewer.

::: notes
The first step with a new table should be inspection rather than immediate filtering or plotting. Printing a few rows, checking structure, and looking at variable names usually reveals the row meaning, key candidates, and suspicious column types quickly.
:::

## Ask five questions to understand the data

- What is one observation/row?
- What variables define the key?
- Which columns:
  - identify?
  - measure?
  - label?

## Count rows and columns

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
nrow(panel_df)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column-fragment
ncol(panel_df)
```

## Get variable names

```{r}
#| output-location: default
names(panel_df)
```

## Data key

The key is a set of columns that **uniquely** identifies one observation

- `municipality_code + year`
- Not municipality name (a label)

## Identifier versus label

- Code = identifier
- Name = label
- Identifier for matching
- Label for humans

::: notes
It can be the same column. We could also use `factor()` to assign human-readable labels to the stored identifier codes. The key point is to not rely on labels as identifiers. They could be duplicated, misspelled, or changed over time. Categories should use underlying codes as identifiers.
:::

## Leading zeroes matter

```{r}
#| output-location: default
str(panel_df)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df <- read.csv(
  "../lecture_1/lecture_1_demo_panel.csv",
  colClasses = c(municipality_code = "character")
)
str(panel_df)
```

::: aside
read.csv guesses that "municipality_code" is numeric because it only contains numbers. But if its an identifier the leading zeroes matter and we need to make sure to tell R to read it as character. That is what the `colClasses` argument does in the `read.csv()` call.
:::

# Subsetting Tables

## A table column is just a vector

`$` pulls the column out, then `[]` subsets that vector like before

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df$year[1]
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df$year[1:5]
```

::: notes
This is the key bridge. After a column has been extracted from the table, subsetting works exactly like it does on any other vector.
:::

## On data.frame: `[]` keeps table, `[[]]`, `$` pulls vector

`[]` returns a one-column `data.frame`

```{r}
head(panel_df["year"])
```

`[[]]` returns the vector inside

```{r}
head(panel_df[["year"]])
```

::: notes
This distinction is about returned shape more than about internal storage. Keeping the table shape is useful when further table operations should still work on the result as a table.
:::

## Subsetting both rows and columns with `[]`

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df[1:3, c("municipality_name", "year")]
```

- First slot = rows
- Second slot = columns

## Filter with logic

Works just like vector filtering, but keeps the table shape:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df[
  panel_df$year == 2023 &
  panel_df$municipality_name %in% c("Stockholm", "Uppsala", "Kiruna"),
  c("municipality_name", "year", "unemployment_rate")
]
```

## Filtering keeps row meaning

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df[
  panel_df$municipality_code %in% c("0180", "0380", "1280") &
  panel_df$year %in% c(2022, 2023),
]
```

- Fewer rows
- Same observation
- Note `,` at the end to keep all columns

# Working With Table Columns

## Assigning to a new column

We can create a new column by assigning to a column name that doesn't exist yet:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df$high_unemployment <- panel_df$unemployment_rate > 8
head(panel_df[c("municipality_name", "unemployment_rate", "high_unemployment")])
```

::: aside
The `unemployment_rate` column is a vector, and the comparison (`> 8`) is vectorized. The operation evaluates to a logical vector of the same length as the original column, and the result stays aligned row by row with the original table.
:::

## `ifelse()` can build categories

```{r}
#| output-location: default
panel_df$period <- ifelse(panel_df$year >= 2020, "recent", "older")
head(panel_df[c("year", "period")])
```

::: notes
`ifelse()` is often useful for creating quick derived categories from existing columns. Because the output is a vector of the same length, it can be added back to the table as a new column.
:::

# Categories

## `factor()` creates categorical data

A factor is a vector of integer levels with attached labels

```{r}
kon <- c(1L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 2L)
typeof(kon)
```

```{r}
kon <- kon |>
  factor(
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("Male", "Female")
  )
typeof(kon)
```

```{r}
class(kon)
```

```{r}
str(kon)
```

```{r}
kon
```

## A factor in a table

```{r}
sex_demo <- data.frame(
  id = 1:4,
  sex_code = c(1, 2, 1, 2)
)
sex_demo$sex <- factor(
  sex_demo$sex_code,
  levels = c(1, 2),
  labels = c("Male", "Female")
)
sex_demo
```

## What a factor stores

- Numeric codes
- Human labels
- Explicit categories

::: aside
Factors attach labels to stored codes. Factors look like labeled text when printed, but internally they store integer codes plus a set of levels. This saves lots of memory and is useful for various reasons. But factors behave differently from plain character columns sometimes and need a bit of caution.
:::

# Tidy Data

## Tidy data

Tidy data is a standard way of organizing tables that makes them easier to work with. The tidy data principles are simple but powerful, and they apply to almost any kind of data.

![&nbsp;](../lecture_1/tidy-data.png)

::: notes
This picture gives the compact rule behind tidy data: columns correspond to variables, rows correspond to observations, and each cell contains one value. The rest of the section just makes that rule concrete with examples.
:::

## Tidy data rule

- One row per observation
- One column per variable
- One cell per value

## Wide table: year in the column name

```{r}
#| output-location: default
wide_rates <- data.frame(
  municipality_code = c("0180", "0380", "1280"),
  unemployment_rate_2022 = c(10.5, 10.2, 18.0),
  unemployment_rate_2023 = c(10.5, 9.9, 17.7)
)
wide_rates
```

## Tidy table: year as a variable

```{r}
#| output-location: default
tidy_rates <- data.frame(
  municipality_code = c("0180", "0180", "0380", "0380", "1280", "1280"),
  year = c(2022, 2023, 2022, 2023, 2022, 2023),
  unemployment_rate = c(10.5, 10.5, 10.2, 9.9, 18.0, 17.7)
)
tidy_rates
```

## Same question, two table shapes

Both tables contain the same information, but one is easier to work with:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
wide_rates[c("municipality_code", "unemployment_rate_2023")]
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
tidy_rates[tidy_rates$year == 2023, c("municipality_code", "unemployment_rate")]
```

## Why tidy usually wins

- Same code across years
- Easier filtering
- Easier joining
- Easier plotting

# Basic Checks

## Check names and types

Before filtering or plotting, check the boring structure first:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
names(panel_df)[1:6]
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
str(panel_df)
```

- Names reveal variable content
- Types reveal how `R` will treat the column

## Check the range

Summary statistics catch implausible values quickly:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
summary(panel_df$unemployment_rate)
```

- Minimum and maximum
- Center and spread
- Anything implausible?

## Check missing values

Then count missingness explicitly:

```{r}
#| output-location: default
sum(is.na(panel_df$unemployment_rate))
```

- Missing values?
- Count first
- Investigate next

## Check the key

```{r}
#| output-location: default
any(duplicated(panel_df[c("municipality_code", "year")]))
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
head(panel_df[c("municipality_code", "year")])
```

## Break the table on purpose

```{r}
#| output-location: default
bad_panel <- panel_df[c(1, 2, 3, 4, 1), ]
bad_panel$unemployment_rate[2] <- NA
```

- One missing value
- One duplicated key

## Check the broken example

```{r}
#| output-location: default
is.na(bad_panel$unemployment_rate)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
duplicated(bad_panel[c("municipality_code", "year")])
```

```{r}
#| output-location: default
any(duplicated(bad_panel[c("municipality_code", "year")]))
```

## Filter out missing rows

```{r}
#| output-location: default
bad_panel[!is.na(bad_panel$unemployment_rate), ]
```

- Keep observed rows
- Drop missing values explicitly

## Checklist for a new table

- Row meaning
- Key
- Unique key?
- Right types?
- Missing values?

::: notes
This checklist separates structure questions from value questions. Both matter before any serious analysis starts.
:::

# Quick Inspection Plots

## Why plot now?

Simple plots are useful long before polished visualization:

- Check data fast
- Use in problem sets
- Better design in lecture 10

## Three quick plot patterns

- `hist(x)`
- `boxplot(x)`
- `plot(x, y)`

## Histogram

```{r}
#| output-location: default
hist(
  panel_df$unemployment_rate,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Municipal unemployment rates",
  xlab = "Unemployment rate"
)
```

## Quick boxplot

```{r}
#| output-location: default
boxplot(
  formula = unemployment_rate ~ year,
  data = panel_df[panel_df$year >= 2020, ],
  xlab = "Year",
  ylab = "Unemployment rate"
)
```

## Quick scatterplot

```{r}
#| output-location: default
plot(
  x = panel_df$year,
  y = panel_df$unemployment_rate,
  xlab = "Year",
  ylab = "Unemployment rate"
)
```

## Main takeaways

- Vectors support element-wise work
- Vectorization often avoids explicit repetition
- Tables are lists of equal-length vectors
- Keys and identifiers matter
- Tidy helps repeated work
- Check early
- Plot early
